Added 2026-08-24 after CI flagged it as new on the v0.9.6 post-release commit. Not a compiler bug -- a deliberate, documented tradeoff: detach() (src/backend_c.rs's TypedStmt::Detach codegen) intentionally leaks the task's heap-allocated ctx struct, since nobody ever joins to free it and the outline function is shared with join's codegen (which still needs ctx alive after the thread exits). Whether LeakSanitizer's exit-time reachability scan actually flags this leak is a genuine race against the detached thread's own lifetime: if the (trivial, no-sleep) thread has already exited and its stack -- which held the only pointer to ctx -- is gone by scan time, the block is truly unreachable and gets flagged; if the thread is still running (or its stack frame lingers in glibc's thread-stack cache), the pointer is still reachable and LSan stays quiet. Locally reproduced this as genuinely nondeterministic: 10 runs of the exact leak_sweep.py-flagged binary gave 9 clean + 1 leaked. Marked "flaky" so a run where it doesn't reproduce isn't treated as a stale baseline entry.

BUG-232, found 2026-08-30 by CI immediately after commit 0a41a48d fixed this same file's original double-free (BUG-201 proper): fixing the double-free let the program run to completion for the first time, which is what let LeakSanitizer's exit-time scan actually observe this SEPARATE, pre-existing leak underneath it -- masked until now by the crash. Root cause: an affine closure's heap-allocated env struct (malloc'd in backend_c.rs's is_aff constructor path) is only freed via two mechanisms -- (1) TypedStmt::Drop at the owning LOCAL BINDING's scope exit (checker.rs's emit_current_scope_drops, gated on CLOSURE_AFF_REGISTRY containing that binding's NAME), or (2) the direct-call save/null/free sequence when the binding is called immediately as `name(args)`. Neither fires here: `add_n` is passed BY VALUE into `apply(add_n, 5)` rather than called directly, which the checker's move-tracking treats as ownership transferring into the callee -- correctly suppressing the caller-side Drop -- but `apply`'s own parameter `f` is never registered in CLOSURE_AFF_REGISTRY (that registry is populated only at a closure LITERAL's creation site, keyed by the local name given there, and has no mechanism to propagate through a function-call boundary to a differently-named callee parameter). The callee can't infer this on its own either: `Closure(i64) -> i64` is one type regardless of whether a given call site's actual argument is heap-backed (affine) or stack-backed (`static __thread`, the Copy-capture case) -- freeing unconditionally on scope exit would double-free/corrupt the common stack-backed case. A correct general fix needs the closure ABI itself to carry a runtime own-vs-borrowed tag (e.g. a third fat-pointer field) so any scope, including a callee's parameter scope, can safely decide whether to free -- a real design change touching every constructor and Drop site, not a local patch, and exactly the kind of rushed-ABI-change risk that produced the original double-free this same file was named for. Deliberately triaged (not fixed) for that reason; tracked for a dedicated follow-up round in docs/TODO_CURRENT.md.

Round-8 audit (2026-08-09), triaged low severity, not fixed: the C backend emits vani's i64::MIN literal as `-(int64_t)9223372036854775808LL`, technically UB by the strict C standard (huge-unsigned-to-int64_t conversion + negating an unrepresentable value), but universally implemented as the intended two's-complement value via constant folding on every real compiler/CPU. The program's actual overflow-check logic (__builtin_add_overflow + abort()) is present and correct; this is purely about how the literal itself is spelled in the generated C, not a missing runtime check. No observed wrong output.

Round-8 audit (2026-08-09), triaged low severity, not fixed: UBSan reports 'left shift ... cannot be represented' -- vani's `<<` is meant to be a raw, always-well-defined bitwise operation, but the C backend emits it as C's native `<<` on a signed int64_t, which has stricter letter-of-the-standard UB rules when the shifted result doesn't fit. Universally implemented as a single machine SHL instruction in practice; no observed wrong output.
